newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK house prices seen up 8.5 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK house prices seen up 8.5 pct in 1997.

text.p: House prices in Britain look set to climb more than eight percent this year, with only a slight easing in growth in 1998, as too many people chase too few homes, a Reuters survey of property price forecasts showed on Wednesday.
The median forecast from 20 banks, research houses and building societies surveyed on Tuesday and Wednesday pointed to an 8.5 percent rise in prices in 1997.

In 1998, analysts expect 1997's rises to attract more properties to the market. That, combined with anticipated higher interest rates, should slow growth to seven percent, an average of 19 forecasts showed.

A strapping economy has spawned a robust consumer sector which is fuelling demand for housing in Britain, a country where home ownership is traditionally high. A lack of suitable properties on the market is also pushing up prices. "There is continued potential strength this year in terms of real disposable pay," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.

"A tightening labour market is pushing wages up, and consumers will benefit from windfall gains from building society conversions -- it's enough to see growth in the housing market." Miller predicted house prices would rise by nine percent in 1997.

Would-be buyers are competing for a handful of saleable properties at reasonable prices, analysts said. A recent report by Black Horse Agencies said for every house coming on to the market, there were nine buyers signing up with estate agents.
"Supply has been an issue. There just aren't enough houses," said Stuart Wetherby, Panmure Gordon's UK economist.

"One of the things that drove housing in the early 1980s was first time buyers from the baby boom," he said. "People are getting older and looking for three-bedroom detached houses which just aren't on the market and this is exasperating the bear squeeze."

Last year, borrowers were spoiled for choice with banks and building societies falling over themselves to lend money for property, analysts said. But this prompted a surge in demand and has cleared out many estate agents.

Aggravating this further is the stubborn problem of negative equity -- where the mortgage on the property exceeds its current market value -- as well as the general level of indebtedness in the personal sector.
Brendan Baker, economist at Lombard Street Research said debt, although diminishing, was still prevalent and was preventing people from putting their homes on the market.
Nevertheless, the number of transactions should increase throughout 1997 as pent-up demand to move hits the market and prices rise, enabling more home-owners to emerge from the negative equity trap.
This, combined with a likely interest rate rise in Britain after the election on May 1, would dampen the market in 1998. The base rate currently stands at six percent.

"Interest rates have troughed and we could have more increases by the end of the year. Seven percent is not an outlandish estimate. A quarter-point increase will not have an enormous effect but a full percentage point will make some people flinch," said Baker.

While analysts said the increase in rates and the consequent economic slowdown would dampen housing growth, they stressed that rates were still comparatively low and growth would remain strong and sustainable.

"Affordability is still very good. Even if interest rates go up this year they'll still be very low by historical standards," said Martin Ellis, economist at the Woolwich Building Society. He predicted a six percent rise over 1997, slowing to five percent over 1998.
